question:
I'm CTO at a 140-person logistics SaaS. Three product lines, one engineering group of about 60 in nine squads. Every sprint overflows: we plan around 40 points, ship 25, and carry the rest into the next one. Marketing wants a feature a week for the growth push and says quality is engineering's problem; engineering says the churn numbers come from bugs. My head of engineering has set a "stretch" target of 40% more throughput by Q1 and tied the squad leads' bonus to it. Most developers sit on two or three squads at once, because the CEO's rule is that nobody is idle. Last month a bad release took the customer portal down for four hours; the postmortem named the developer who merged it, and he's now on a performance plan. The CEO's answer to all of this is to buy AI coding tools so we can "do both".

I need a two-page memo for the CEO that says what's actually going on here, what to change first and why that first, and where the thinking you're drawing on disagrees with itself.

Answer here in the chat.
text:
MEMORANDUM
TO: Chief Executive Officer
FROM: Chief Technology Officer
DATE: October 31, 2026
SUBJECT: Systemic Diagnostic & Strategic Action Plan: Engineering Flow, Quality, and Operational Governance
Executive Summary & Diagnostic: "What Is Actually Going On Here"
Our current operational crisis—sprint overruns, escalating churn from production bugs, department friction, and recent outages—is not caused by developer apathy or insufficient coding speed. It is the predictable result of a systemic design failure. We are running our software organization on flawed operational assumptions that systematically generate bottleneck queues, incentivize quality compromises, and create severe single-point failures[1][2][3].
Below is the systemic diagnosis across four key organizational dynamics:
1. The Utilization Trap & Queuing Chaos (Operating as a Resource Topology)
Our rule that "nobody is idle," which splits developers across two or three squads simultaneously, is the primary driver of our delivery collapse[3][4]. In organizational design terminology, we are operating in a Resource Topology—a model that attempts to maximize local labor utilization ("keeping people 100% busy") rather than value flow[3][5].
Queuing Theory (Little’s Law) dictates that as resource utilization approaches 100%, queue times and lead times increase exponentially (Cycle Time=WIP/Throughput)[6]. By forcing engineers onto multiple squads, we inflate Work-In-Progress (WIP) and generate massive context-switching overhead[4][7].
Furthermore, software development communication overhead grows non-linearly with team interdependencies (D
peak
	​

 thresholds)[8]. Because our 60 engineers are fragmented across 9 squads, individual focus is destroyed, handover friction spikes, and velocity stalls[4][7][8]. A system with 100% busy people inevitably yields 0% flow efficiency[3][9].
2. Goodhart’s Law & Perverse Incentives (The 40% Stretch Target)
Tying squad leads' bonuses to an arbitrary "stretch" target of 40% more throughput by Q1 triggers Goodhart’s Law: "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure"[10][11].
Expecting a clogged system to deliver 40% more throughput forces engineers into an Efficiency-Thoroughness Trade-Off (ETTO)[12]. When output volume is tied to financial compensation, teams systematically sacrifice thoroughness—skipping automated testing, truncating code reviews, and taking architectural shortcuts[12][13][14].
The result is a surge in technical debt and production defects[15]. Marketing correctly observes that churn is driven by bugs, but engineering is being explicitly incentivized to generate those bugs to meet volume targets[13][14][15][16].
3. The Blame Cycle vs. Systemic Safety (The Postmortem Failure)
Placing the developer who merged the bad release on a Performance Improvement Plan (PIP) is a critical organizational mistake[17][18].
Human Performance Improvement (HPI) and Just Culture research demonstrate that human error is a symptom of underlying system weakness, not the root cause[1][2][19]. Blaming the individual ("the sharp end") creates a false illusion that the problem is solved while leaving the latent organizational pathogens—unclear rollback procedures, missing automated integration tests, and fatigue—completely intact[2][17][20].
Disciplining staff for honest operational errors initiates a destructive Blame Cycle[18][21]. It destroys psychological safety, encourages developers to hide near-misses, stifles open communication, and destroys the reporting culture required to prevent catastrophic outages[21][22][23][24][25].
4. AI Coding Tools as a "Fix That Fails"
Investing in AI coding tools as a standalone solution to "do both" (increase throughput and maintain quality) represents the classic system archetype Fixes that Fail[26][27].
AI tools accelerate localized code generation ("doing" tasks)[28]. However, if we feed more code into a pipeline blocked by multi-squad dependencies, manual testing, and high WIP, AI will simply generate buggy code faster[3][15][29]. AI cannot solve a structural queueing and alignment problem[3][30].
Prioritized Action Plan: "What to Change First and Why That First"
To restore operational stability, we must apply the Theory of Constraints (TOC): "Any improvements made anywhere besides the bottleneck are an illusion"[31][32][33].
[Phase 1: Unblock Bottleneck] ──► [Phase 2: Remove Perverse Incentives] ──► [Phase 3: Institute Just Culture] ──► [Phase 4: Strategic AI]
  • Eliminate Multi-Squads        • Cancel 40% Throughput Bonus           • Reverse Developer PIP              • Target Automated Gates
  • Enforce Strict WIP Limits     • Implement Flow & Quality Metrics       • Blameless Postmortems              • Elevate Skill Mandate

Step 1: Eliminate Multi-Squad Allocation & Limit WIP (Immediate Priority)
Action: Immediately ban multi-squad assignment. Mandate that every developer belongs to exactly one squad. Restructure the 60 engineers into dedicated, stable teams aligned to clear product capabilities, and establish strict WIP limits across all product backlogs[4][7][34][35].
Why First?: Multi-squad context-switching is our single greatest system bottleneck[4][7]. Until we stop task-switching and clear the clogged pipeline, no amount of target-setting, process changes, or AI tools will increase output[31][32]. Single-squad dedication instantly reduces WIP, lowers context-switching costs, and restores predictable flow[4][6][36].
Step 2: De-Link Bonuses from Throughput & Align on Flow/Quality Metrics
Action: Cancel the 40% throughput bonus target for squad leads. Replace sprint velocity targets with Flow Metrics (Lead Time, Cycle Time, Defect Escape Rate) and shared customer outcomes co-owned by Product, Marketing, and Engineering[9][10][37][38][39].
Why Second: Once WIP is capped, we must remove the perverse financial incentives driving Goodhart's Law gaming, point-inflation, and quality cutting[10][11][16].
Step 3: Transition to a Just Culture & Institute Blameless Postmortems
Action: Reverse the PIP for the developer involved in the portal outage. Implement James Reason's Culpability Decision Tree and the Substitution Test ("Would another engineer with similar training have made the same error under those exact system pressures?") for all postmortems[40][41][42][43][44]. Shift investment toward automated deployment guardrails and pre-release verification testing[1][45][46].
Why Third: Unclogging the workflow requires transparent reporting[25][47]. Rebuilding psychological safety ensures engineers report system flaws and production risks early without fear of retribution[22][23][25].
Step 4: Deploy AI Strategically to Elevate Team Capabilities
Action: Shift our AI investment from general code generation to automating our specific delivery constraints—such as automated regression test suite generation, pull-request verification, and deployment pipeline checks[29][30].
Why Fourth: Guided by Org Topologies, AI should be used to broaden our teams' skills mandate and work mandate, elevating them toward cross-functional, end-to-end delivery units[30][35][48][49][50].
Theoretical Disagreements: Tensions & Nuance in the Management Science
To make an informed decision, we must acknowledge where the foundational management theories we are drawing upon disagree with one another:
Strategic Area
	
Theoretical Tension
	
Core Contradiction in Literature
	
Resolution for Our SaaS Context


Goal Setting vs. Process Quality
	
Goal-Setting Theory (Locke & Latham) vs. Total Quality Management (TQM) (Deming)
	
Goal-Setting Theory argues that difficult, specific "stretch" goals drive higher motivation and effort[51][52][53]. Deming and TQM counter that numerical stretch targets narrow vision, induce fear, invite cheating, and destroy process quality[54][55][56].
	
Stretch goals work for simple, independent tasks; in complex software engineering, aggressive numerical targets induce systemic gaming under Goodhart's Law[10][14][54]. We must adopt Deming's focus on continuous process improvement over arbitrary velocity quotas[54][55].


Resource Efficiency vs. Flow Efficiency
	
Scientific Management (Taylorism) vs. Lean / Queuing Theory
	
Classical Management prioritizes 100% labor utilization ("nobody is idle") to maximize resource cost-efficiency[3][57][58]. Lean and Queuing Theory prove that 100% capacity utilization causes infinite queue delays, destroyed flow, and higher overall costs[3][6][9][39].
	
In software delivery, optimizing for human utilization destroys value flow[9][39]. We must intentionalize capacity slack so work items can move rapidly without waiting in queues[4][6][39].


Individual Accountability vs. System Safety
	
Strict Individual Accountability vs. Just Culture / Blameless Safety
	
Pure "blameless" models posit that human errors are 100% system-induced and individual discipline is always counterproductive[24][59][60][61][62]. Just Culture frameworks (Reason, DOE HPI) distinguish between honest human error and reckless, intentional violations[18][40][63][64].
	
We must reject individual scapegoating for honest errors while maintaining clear accountability for adherence to workable, agreed-upon engineering safety standards[18][40][63][65].


AI Value Model
	
Micro-Efficiency vs. Strategic Organizational Elevation
	
Conventional executive views see AI as an individual labor-saving tool (writing syntax faster)[28]. Org Topologies demonstrates that localized speedups in "doing" tasks without expanding team scope or removing dependencies merely compound downstream bottlenecks[3][29][66].
	
AI investment must focus on expanding team capabilities to eliminate dependencies, not padding task-level coding speed[29][30].
Summary Recommendation
By ending multi-squad matrixing, capping Work-in-Progress, replacing velocity quotas with flow/quality metrics, and establishing a Just Culture, we can stabilize our customer portal, reduce bug-driven churn, and create a sustainable delivery engine[4][6][25][34][40].
💡 Next Step: Would you like me to prepare an implementation matrix mapping out squad realignments, WIP limit thresholds, and replacement flow metrics for our upcoming leadership meeting?

1.chunk: It is not easy to anticipate exactly how trivial conditions can influence individual performance. Error-provoking aspects of facility*1 design, procedures, processes, and human nature exist everywhere. No matter how efficiently equipment functions; how good the training, supervision, and procedures; and how well the best worker, engineer, or manager performs his or her duties, people cannot perform better than the organization supporting them.1 Human error is caused not only by normal human fallibility, but also by incompatible management and leadership practices and organizational weaknesses in work processes and values. Therefore, defense-in-depth with respect to the human element is needed to improve the resilience of programmatic systems and to drive down human error and events.

2.chunk: In 1997, Reason published Managing the Risks of Organizational Accidents. Reason maintained that to understand how organizational accidents occur requires that we look deeper into the system. Unsafe acts by individuals may trigger an event. However, latent conditions within the organization, aligned with local workplace and task factors, contribute to accidents in the form of process errors or as error-likely situations. Thus it is the combination of these latent conditions in conjunction with an active error that more correctly accounts for events. From this perspective, errors are the consequences, not the causes, of disturbances in the organization. Accidents are the result of failed controls and barriers. People are fallible, even the best make mistakes. It is human nature to err. However, events can be eliminated or controlled by changing the conditions in which people work. Managing the risks of organizational accidents requires that managers, supervisors, and staff work to eliminate latent organizational weaknesses. Reason proposes three compelling reasons why latent conditions have to be eliminated.

3.chunk:
Resource Topology There are three common Org Topologies to know, starting  with: The Resource Topology—​a topology characterized by  frozen functional archetypes specialized in one domain. Its  purpose is to ensure that each unit is 100% utilized (i.e.  resource utilization). It is seen in “resource management”  approaches where “resource managers” (or project  managers) are responsible for planning and monitoring  resource allocation and utilization.
In this topology, the value-​creation work takes place among  the Doing Archetypes in the lower left quadrant. However,  none of these can independently produce end-​to-​end  customer value. They depend on each other due to narrow  specialization. Additionally, they lack a clear and holistic  understanding of customer value, as their work mandate  focuses solely on specific tasks or capabilities.

Reduce the Batch Size of your Efforts Research in the way the mind works, and countless experiences from Lean, the Theory of Constraints and Kanban confirm that to deliver value faster, with better flow and good team morale we need to focus and limit the number of things we do. Multitasking does not work. Limiting how many things you do at any given time, means reducing the batch size of whatever you are doing at a particular stage of the value chain. By doing this you will deliver value faster because you are able to focus your efforts, one of the best explanations of this fact has been given by Donald G. Reinertsen. Keeping the team focused helps them finish what they start faster. Limiting WIP is a consequence of reducing the batch size of your efforts, and not the other way around. However doing either will result in improvements in efficiency and productivity. Open Kanban does not ask you to limit WIP, but it does request that you “Reduce the Batch Size of your Efforts.” How do you reduce the batch size of your efforts? Reduce the complexity and the quantity of things you do at any stage of the value chain. In software development this would mean: reduce the number of large stories (epics) you create, and do your best to keep stories simple; also reduce the volume of stories you work on any stage of the Software Development Life Cycle; this way your team will focus, and deliver more value.

Another dysfunctional result of poor control systems can be seen in their effect on goal-setting programs. Whereas a good control system can help design and monitor valuable goal-setting programs, a poor control system can accomplish quite the opposite. INVESTIGATING EVENTS TRIGGERED BY HUMAN ERROR
Overview A traditional view of events and accidents is that they are caused by shortcomings in human competence, attention, or attitude. It may be under the label of “loss of situation awareness,” procedural “violation,” or “poor” management. A new and different view is that human error is not the cause of failure, but a symptom of failure—trouble deeper inside the system. Human error is not the chief threat to system safety, but rather latent organizational conditions set the stage for error and determine the severity of the consequences. Human error is not just random. It is tied to features of people’s tools, the tasks they perform, and the operating environment in which they work. In this perspective, human error is not the conclusion but rather the starting point of investigations. The point of these investigations should be to prevent recurrence, not simply to find people to punish.

The “shifting the burden” archetype shows what happens when we address the symptoms of a problem with a quick-fix solution. This solution is easier and faster than creating an upstream solution to the problem, and we are often meeting a very real, urgent need for a student. The second basic premise is that difficult goals result in better performance than easy goals. This does not mean that difficult goals are always achieved, but our performance will usually be better when we intend to achieve harder goals. Your goal of an A in Classical Mechanics at Cal Tech may not get you your A, but it may earn you a B+, which you wouldn’t have gotten otherwise. Difficult goals cause us to exert more effort, and this almost always results in better performance.
Another premise of goal theory is that specific goals are better than vague goals. We often wonder what we need to do to be successful. Have you ever asked a professor “What do I need to do to get an A in this course?” If she responded “Do well on the exams,” you weren’t much better off for having asked. This is a vague response. Goal theory says that we perform better when we have specific goals. Had your professor told you the key thrust of the course, to turn in all the problem sets, to pay close attention to the essay questions on exams, and to aim for scores in the 90s, you would have something concrete on which to build a strategy.

Had your professor told you the key thrust of the course, to turn in all the problem sets, to pay close attention to the essay questions on exams, and to aim for scores in the 90s, you would have something concrete on which to build a strategy.

53.chunk: Goal-Setting Theory Goal-setting theory is based on the premise that an individual’s intention to work toward a goal is a primary source of motivation. Once set, the goal clarifies for the employee what needs to be accomplished and how much effort will be required for completion. The theory has three main components: (1) specific goals lead to a higher level of performance than do more generalized goals (“do your best”); (2) more difficult goals lead to better performance than do easy goals (provided the individual accepts the goal); and (3) feedback on progress toward the goal enhances performance. Feedback is particularly important because it helps the individual identify the gap between the real (the actual performance) and the ideal (the desired outcome defined by the goal). Given the trend toward employee empowerment in the workplace, more and more employees are participating in the goal-setting process.

54.chunk: The Negative Side of Goals There is, however, a negative side to goal setting. Total quality management (TQM) pioneer W. Edwards Deming fears that goals tend to narrow the performer’s vision and invite people to slack off once the goal is achieved. TQM is also oriented more toward process (means) than toward success (goals, outcomes). Organizational learning and continuous improvement, a central component of TQM, is oriented toward continually finding problems in the production process that when eliminated will result in performance increases.40 Performance goals, on the other hand, generally focus the performer’s attention on successfully achieving a specified level of accomplishment at some future point.

Dr. W. Edwards Deming, an American management consultant, was the first to say that quality control should be a company-wide goal. His ideas were adopted by the Japanese in the 1950s but largely ignored in the United States until the 1970s. Deming believed that quality control starts with top management, who must foster a company-wide culture dedicated to producing quality.
Deming’s concept of Total Quality Management (TQM) emphasizes the use of quality principles in all aspects of a company’s production and operations. It recognizes that all employees involved with bringing a product or service to customers—marketing, purchasing, accounting, shipping, manufacturing—contribute to its quality. Managing through Goal Setting What can managers do to motivate employees through goal setting? First, it is important to encourage goal acceptance and commitment. This can be accomplished by working with organizational members to set difficult, specific, and reasonable goals and to make certain that members perceive them as reasonable. If necessary, provide training and other support needed to make the goals attainable. Offer feedback that lets people know when they are approaching the goal. Avoid using threats. Feedback that criticizes without providing insight into ways to contribute to performance improvements is both frustrating and unlikely to be effective. One of Deming’s concerns about goal setting is that it creates fear in employees—fear of the failure to reach the goal. He sees fear as a serious disease that contributes to poor organizational performance.46

A postmortem typically also covers incident timeline and all factors that in a given organization generate incident, and impacts operators behavior before, during and after the outage has happened. Practice allows participants and stakeholders to quickly form conclusions on what were the most important factors contributing to the incident. It also serves a learning purpose, both by providing in depth experience for participants and by producing a postmortem summary which can be shared with all interested parties. A postmortem can be treated as the evolution of a Root Cause Analysis (RCA) which is done in almost all major IT support organizations.

64.chunk: The line between acceptable and unacceptable behavior is more clear when the logic diagram is used. An intentional act to cause harm (lower left) is wholly unacceptable and should receive very severe sanctions, possibly administered by the courts rather than the organization. Knowingly violating expectations that were workable likely suggests reckless violation, a condition that warrants sanctions. The remaining categories should be thought of as blameless— unless they involve aggravating factors not considered here. Experience suggests that the majority of unsafe acts—perhaps 90 percent or more—fall into the blameless category.35
